utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Ms. Udo for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, representing the Defence for Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with my colleague, Mr. Michael Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Cynthia McMurrey and, along with me, Ms. Nancy Boler, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Before the witness comes in, may I mention a matter? It relates to the next witness that the Defence proposed to call -- it is the military expert, Brigadier Mohamed Vejzajic. I just wanted to say to the court at this stage, so that your Honours are aware of the position of the Prosecution, we do not expect to be in a position to be able to cross-examine this witness immediately at the conclusion of his evidence. It is a much greater task in relation to this witness, because of the volume of material and the areas that he covers, and so I am just not going to be in a position to be ready to cross-examine -- I can see that now -- and I thought I should tell your Honours. Your Honours, I do not expect any difficulty with this and it is really a matter of formality, but I notice that the Defence have not filed any documentation pursuant to your Honours' order of 25 January 1997 seeking leave to call this witness pursuant to paragraph 4 of your Honours' orders. I do not expect any problem in the Prosecution other than, because of the late receipt of the material, we are not going to be in a position to cross-examine at the ordinary and usual time. That will be our only opposition, should they seek to make such an application. I just note, your Honour, for the record, that no such application has been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you anticipate the nature of the evidence that that witness is likely to give will be other than the ordinary --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is not only the length. It goes to the complexity of the material which really needs to be examined. Initially, when I started out, I did not think I was going to be able to cross-examine, either. By burning the midnight oil, I was able to continue this cross-examination, which I wanted to do. I just see now I am not going to be in a position with the next witness, so I wish to indicate that to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am ready to continue, unless there is a response, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as the right of the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness at another time is concerned, this is a matter for the Trial Chamber. I only want to say that, in accordance with the order of the Trial Chamber, we said that we would examine three witnesses -- an historian, a military expert and a demographer. We did not notify the court, but I want to point out that we are not going to examine the expert on demographic matters. I think that we did provide full information on the two witnesses that we intended to call. However, during the last fall, our original expert witness notified us that he was involved in the events in and around Konjic and that he may not be fully impartial in testifying, so we sought a new witness, and, as far as the information regarding this new military expert is concerned, we notified the Trial Chamber that we would provide the full biographical information for him as soon as we found one. After about a month we did locate a new witness and we felt that it was not necessary for us to ask for a new permission of the Trial Chamber to call a military witness, so we believed that we were still complying with the original order when calling this new witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us have the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt right now but we are having a problem -- LiveNote, the transcript, is not coming up on our computer. I ask the Registry if they could help us work on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would you kindly inform the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I take note of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How soon will you be ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will take about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps while we are waiting the professor could be given his report and his exhibits -- his report and binder. (Handed). TECHNICIAN: This line is broken -- it will not work. I cannot solve it immediately, I will have to do it in the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We are willing to proceed without it as long as we can get it as soon as possible. We do make our notes on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you, you can proceed. ILJAS HADZIBEGOVIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, I wanted to start by asking you some questions about the old structure under the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- just a couple of questions on that. Professor, under that old structure, the position was that the JNA and the Territorial Defence, during times of war, the design was that they would work together; is that right, and that the command of the Territorial Defence would come under the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my report, since I knew that there was a military expert who was going to be called here, I did not particularly deal with the JNA and the Territorial Defence, because I believe that it is the next witness who is going to testify to that in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly, professor, I do not want to take you to things that you are uncomfortable talking about. So, if you feel that it does not happily fit within your expertise, please tell me, and I will move on. I still wanted to ask you some questions, and I will put them to you, but on the understanding, if you feel uncomfortable about answering them, let me know. Would it be correct that the Territorial Defence is, however, very much a local organisation, and was designed to have the capacity to operate independently of the JNA in circumstances where, for example, the JNA was no longer able to function. I am speaking again under the old structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I would like to state that these are theoretical issues, which I have not dealt in, and I am sorry, but I do not feel comfortable about answering this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What you did speak about, however, in your report was the relationship between the Territorial Defence and the local municipal Government -- do you agree with me -- is that right, that you mentioned that and spoke of that in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned the Territorial Defence in a very limited sense -- as part of the Defence of the Konjic municipality and this is something that was the competence of the presidency, and this is the context in which I spoke of the Territorial Defence and I would like to limit myself to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means. I am happy to remain limited to that as well. Do you agree with me that the president of the municipality had authority over the Territorial Defence when it comes to matters of Civil Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please make the question more specific? I am not clear what it is, because the president of the municipality had no command or control authority over the military, including the Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What I am putting to you is that, in terms of Civil Defence -- that is, matters that happened in the municipality relating to natural disasters, flood, fires and things of that nature -- the president of the municipality did have certain authority over the Territorial Defence, or do you deny that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you deny it, or do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian Defence or protection is not the same as Territorial Defence. Civilian protection takes care of the population in extraordinary situations -- floods, earthquakes, disasters, so it is not the same as the Territorial Defence -- it is a separate part of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You are quite right. My question, though, is in terms of civil disaster, such as earthquake, floods and so forth, the president of the municipality has the authority to mobilise and utilise the Territorial Defence in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, civilian protection and, in my view, Territorial Defence, no, but I again would like to stress I did not study this Defence, so yes, they can use the civil protection but not the Territorial Defence, that is the high command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am somewhat confused by your answer. Perhaps you are saying you do not know the answer, which is fine if you do not know the answer, just say so, or are you saying that, no, I am wrong when I put to you that the president can mobilise -- the president of the municipality can mobilise the Territorial Defence in times of civil disaster?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He cannot mobilise Territorial Defence. He can mobilise civilian protection or defence, but he has no authority -- control or authority over the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay, that is your view. Yesterday you were asked certain questions about a document that appeared in your index of documents as D22. What I am asking you is where is the document D22 as is referred to in the index -- not the document that is actually numbered D22, but the one that the index refers to -- where is that? When you find it perhaps you might give us the number at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: D22 -- this document is marked 450.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Looking at the translation I have of that document, 450, and going to the description in the annex D of the document, the description I have in annex D is the report of the Konjic RBH army military police, dated 9 December 1992, on the transfer of detainees from the Celebici prison into the sports gymnasium prison in Konjic. The document you have just shown me is a decision on establishing of the State committee for collecting the facts regarding war crimes. I do not know the date but it looks as though it might be 28 April 1992, which I do not know, you might tell me why you say that document is the one that corresponds to the description in annex D.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am going to object to this line of questioning. It came out clear on my cross yesterday that it is a mistake in the index. That is what the witness said, we all agreed it was a mistake in the index.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you not think the witness can tell us what actually the position is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I thought it had been made clear yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is fairer he gives the evidence instead of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also like to object, because the witness has the annex in Bosnian language, which is correct and it was obvious that a mistake was made in translating the annex -- that became clear yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I did not realise I was doing anything spectacular other than trying to sort out what the document is. I want to ask the professor if he relied on it. I cannot see anything objectionable about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think he might be able to answer the question. It is a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps, professor, what I might do is, rather than hold up the proceedings now, we will proceed with other questions and you might have a look for me -- basically I am trying to find that document. I cannot find it. You might have a look through your report and documents later and see if you can assist us. I will come back to it. Professor, you testified about the number of detainees that were held in the Celebici camp. How did you determine the number of detainees -- how did you go about the process of determining the number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first place, I had the list of persons who had been arrested, who had arms in their possession -- military arms -- and who were interrogated. I looked through a large number of those lists, and interrogations, and brief reports on those interrogations. Personally, I examined about 150 such cases and I saw a list of 105 against whom criminal proceedings were instituted. We have also here the document that was referred to yesterday, which I received towards the end of my work on my report and I only managed to have a few of those certificates translated, the certificates on amnesty, which were issued by the higher court in Mostar, and I do not believe that I have collected all the documentation. Some of it has probably been lost, some of it I just could not obtain, but according to some estimates, one may put the figure between 250 and 300 as the number of people who were arrested and detained and whose guilt was in the process of being established. Many were released and I do not know what happened to those documents on persons who were just arrested, interrogated and released. So, I was unable to establish the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, you referred to a list. Is the list included in your documents that you have tendered to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have included the documents on amnesty that I received, and only several of those have been translated. If your Honours wish, as I consider these documents to be extremely important, these are certificates on amnesty, I can have the others translated, too, within a short time delay and submit them to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That might be helpful, professor, if that could happen. But, for the moment, you might just assist us with some of the issues concerning it. Can you tell us whether all of these documents relate to persons who were detained in Celebici, or do some of them relate to Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Musala also appears as an area in which prisoners were held and I think that they are referred to as well -- these persons -- because they were transferred from Celebici to Musala and other locations and that is why it makes it difficult to establish the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you know they were in fact transferred from Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learnt that later. I had not lived in Konjic, so I could not know, but I knew that Musala was opened as another place of detention. It is a gym in a school in which persons were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. But what I am asking you, professor, is not about it so much as how you came to know about Musala. Was it something that someone told you, or was it documents that you examined, or is it indeed these documents D21 and the D21 bundle of documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learnt about that in Konjic, because I went there to see on the ground where those people were and that is where I learnt about it. I went to the locations themselves and I saw this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also said that you had looked at Institute for the Study of War Crimes documents, where you looked at allegations that were made. Did you actually see formulated allegations against the detainees, or was it merely information that was being collected to suggest that something may have -- that the detainees may have committed some offence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As is customary in my work, I undertook to study all the documentation that I had access to, to establish the number of persons, the charges against them, and, having sifted through all that, 105 persons remained, that is, the persons who -- against whom criminal proceedings were started by the courts, and that is what I consider to be important. It is also important to establish how many persons were detained in all, how many of them had hunting weapons with regular licences -- quite a number of them had such licences -- and then the people who did not have arms but who happened to be in certain locations where they were arrested, so that it is rather uncertain except for the fact that they had military arms, according to their own statements, and that they had been organised and they were putting up armed resistance against the legal authorities. That was for me the most essential factor, and of course the total number of people treated, and I could not establish that number, because of the difficulties in collecting the documentation, in preserving the documentation, and therefore such an estimate is permissible and it is valid until other documents are found which prove otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, your view of it is, justifiably so, provisional, based on the material that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From what you could see, you say that some of the persons interned in Celebici were there because they possessed weapons, some military weapons; others because they possessed hunting rifles, others because they possessed weapons that they had with licences, and other people because they just happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could put it that way, except for this third group, to be in the wrong place at the wrong time -- I am not sure about how many there were in such a position, but these two groups, I agree with the way you described them. It is possible that some people were rounded up who were not armed at that moment -- whether they had thrown away those weapons in the meantime or hidden them somewhere, I cannot be sure about that, but some reason must have existed for arresting people who at that moment did not have any weapons on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That reason, I put to you, professor, could well have included the fact that they were in the wrong place at the wrong time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. The person found without weapons may have had some weapons and thrown them away into shrubs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably this happened -- I do not know that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you read documentation which said things like this, that, as they approached, these people were throwing their weapons away in the grass -- did you see that, professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall exactly all those documents and all the details, because there were many of them. Probably there were among them some of such contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you be able to help us by referring to some of those documents in the material that you provided, which said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps, professor, rather than delay the process now, we might come back to that -- you can have a look through your papers and come back after the adjournment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, you say that most of the prisoners who were detained in Celebici were persons, you say in the first few days -- persons who were mainly those who illegally possessed arms when they were brought to Celebici. Is it not correct that, during the entire time, the persons that were detained in Celebici -- no actual charges were brought against them during the time they were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I am afraid the question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I will make it clear then. My question is that you say in your report that people were arrested and detained in Celebici -- when I say "people", I mean some of the people -- I withdraw that. I will quote directly from your report. You say: "During the first days of the war, the arrested persons were mainly those with whom illegally possessed arms had been found." My question is: in relation to the people who were interned in Celebici prison, is it not a fact that, during the period of their internment, that is, in 1992, no charges were actually filed and brought against those persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, we referred a moment ago to your certificates on amnesty. Is it not the case that some of your certificates could belong to persons who were never detained in Celebici -- you would agree with that, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, these are mostly persons who were in Celebici and who were amnestied by the high court in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: "Mostly" will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: "Mostly" will be sufficient, professor. I take it, professor, that you do not know of any incidences where HVO soldiers or paramilitaries were detained in Celebici during 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But, going on what you said yesterday, they would have been illegally possessing arms, would they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that an equation mark cannot be placed between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry -- I did not understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer was in response to the way I understood your question -- the HVO was within the system of defence of Konjic and the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it was under arms. It defended Bosnia-Herzegovina; it defended Konjic and that HVO was not an illegal institution, nor an illegal army, nor a para-army at that time, because there were armed defence forces consisting of the Territorial Defence, the police, and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. What was the legal foundation for the HVO? Where is it in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina that you find that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was not a question of the constitution but a question of the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina and all the military formations that placed themselves in the service of the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina were legal, because they were defending an independent State -- an internationally recognised State.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Legal because of what reason is the question I am asking you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I just add to this, that, in Konjic, as well, there were Serbs who fought as part of the Territorial Defence and who defended Konjic, whereas others on the other side were attacking it. Therefore, the legitimacy is expressed in the fact that each people and each place has the right to defend itself, if it is attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you do not know, professor, you should just tell me you do not know of any legal foundation for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has given the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (... INAUDIBLE ...) Total defence -- it is everybody's responsibility to defend the land and the HVO was engaged in defending the land. Therefore, they thought it was in possession of illegal weapons. It is related to total defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That position of legality continued, did it, through 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So the HVO was a legally constituted force in 1993 -- they were merely defending their territory, of course, which would make them legal on the basis of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I object. This does not come under the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Cross-examination is at large, your Honour, and I think the question of what is legal and what is illegal is a very important issue for this case, because the whole defence seems to be structured on what they say is the legitimate and legal position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are asking him a legal question. You are not asking him an historical question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is a question of higher State policy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the witness might be able to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There is also an objection on the basis that the counsel is giving evidence when he says they were merely defending their territory. There is no evidence from witnesses in this case to that effect. I object to the question and the way it has been framed, the way counsel is seeking to give evidence as to the activities of the HVO in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will reframe it, differently. Mr. Moran told us about the position in the United States and we heard no objection then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I object to that side bar remark. I was using an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it was explained yesterday sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I was just objecting to the side bar remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, assuming the HVO in 1993 were merely defending their territory when they were assumingly involved in a war against the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they a legal force at that stage -- they were after all defending their territory, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I explained yesterday the position of the legal authorities towards the HVO and I think that is sufficient in view of the fact that I did not continue my report to cover 1993, which would require additional research and analyses -- what happened in 1992, that is the area I can answer about, and I can say that the constitutional court proclaimed certain acts by the HVO and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as anti-constitutional, but that the legal Government did not do anything in that connection, because it was under pressure of the struggle that I referred to yesterday -- I do not want to repeat it -- you have it in the transcript and I think that is enough. As regards 1993, the situation is quite different, and a quite different approach is required.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this would answer all your queries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Professor, the Serb forces in Konjic in 1992 were merely defending their territory, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serb forces were not merely defending their territory. The Serb forces were rebelling against the legal authorities -- they wanted to make a State within a State, and that is what was illegal and what is considered a rebellion against the legal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will pass on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not attacked by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You stated in your report that the war presidency passed decisions to provide necessary medical care to people in the Celebici prison; is that right -- do you remember saying that in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That decision was not never implemented, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, but I know that such a decision was taken. It was addressed to the person, but I do not know whether it was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also state that members of the family could visit arrested persons; do you remember saying that in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that your expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was in Celebici and I asked people who were there and they told me that relatives could come to visit and bring food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you keep a record of those discussions to include in your papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- no, I just -- no, I did not make any kind of minutes or record, but this will probably be confirmed by other witnesses who were contemporaries of those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In your report you stated that the war presidency appointed different kinds of coordinators; do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you rely on any documentation for that proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I relied on what I found, and I found that Zejnil Delalic was appointed coordinator of the war presidency in cooperation with the defence forces, the TO, the HVO and the police -- he was meant to coordinate the work between the war presidency and these segments of the defence of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is not quite my question, professor. My question was directed to the different kinds of coordinators -- not specifically Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I also found another fact about coordination within the system of communications between the communications centre and the PTT service -- there, too, a coordinator was appointed, and the HVO, in some cases, also appointed its own coordinators.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was that fact contained in a document, or was it again something someone told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a document about what I have said regarding the communication centre and the post office -- the PTT service, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This deals with the appointment of different kinds of coordinators, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and all of them -- these appointed by the presidency, such a coordinator had mostly logistic tasks, and to engage in various procurements and supplies and to regulate various other matters, including procurement of military materiel and, in this connection, I came across quite a number of documents, whereby the coordinator is instructed to purchase such materiel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you show us where they are in your appendices -- just take us to them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have here the English version. Could I be given the version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, are you in any case doubting whether such an appointment was made?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am very curious to find out the document basis of it, your Honour. I think it is certainly relevant -- the professor has mentioned it and it becomes significant, considering that the issue of coordinator is something of some substance to this case. I am just asking him if he can help me by pointing to what he is relying on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are actually not disputing the accused was appointed coordinator of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is considerable dispute about the roles and functions, your Honour. It may be that we can gain no benefit from it, but it may be we can glean some insight into this issue from looking at other coordinators and what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought you had already given your own evidence to the nature of this appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is not that one we are talking about -- it is the others. The professor has mentioned them and surely I am permitted to ask him to tell us what he relied on. That is all I am asking, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have the contents in the Serbo-Croatian Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We can come back to this after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have only the contents page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We can come back to this, professor. Professor, you mentioned that you had access to a number of documents that were supplied to you by the Defence -- do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have your own copies of these documents, or did you just review the Defence files?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had copies of documents, which I analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they your own copies, or were they the Defence -- did they retain possession of them and you just looked at them, or did you keep copies yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The question is not clear. Are you saying the documents were supplied by the Defence or documents independently obtained by him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I sound confusing I will correct that. The point I want to know, professor, is did the Defence give you access to their documents to look at, and which you reviewed but did not keep a copy of, or did they give you documents, copies of documents which you kept yourself, or is it a mixture of both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could keep the copies for myself. I could just simply keep them and analyse them and use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that some of the documents that you saw you did not put in your appendix of documents -- that is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible, it is possible. I did not say -- I cannot recall which ones I did not include, but of those that I did include, I think that they are all relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In forming your opinion, which you came to when you wrote your report, when you formed your opinion, did you rely on any documents which you did not put in the appendices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether I can answer that question unequivocally, because an opinion is never formed just simply on the exact number of documents that are being presented into evidence. I think that a much wider basis of documents is always used and then you just fill in the gaps, so I did use other material which I have not enclosed here, that was not submitted here, and that it did contribute to forming a full picture of what I presented. But none of that was crucial or essential -- none of that would have changed my views.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, I think what you are saying is we can safely assume that any document which is important, upon which you formed an opinion, is contained in this appendix -- is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned in your report that -- on the last page of your report, that the International Committee of the Red Cross prepared a report and it made certain findings; do you remember saying that? It is the very last line, professor, of the report on page -- the very last page, the very last line, and you say: "According to the findings of the ICRC report and other organisations, some other measures were undertaken for the improvement of the conditions in the prison." Do you see that -- the very last sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please -- are you referring to my expert's report, or the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The expert report, the very last sentence of your expert report -- the very last page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The family visits were allowed according to the findings of the commission of the ICRC and other measures were taken to improve the conditions in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you see that there? Professor, did you have access to this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This, I found out separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How can you comment on the findings of a report that you never read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the way that the reports are used -- that is the reports that appear in the media, and this is how such reports were interpreted, and so that is also a way to form an opinion, so my position is that the finding of the commission was that certain improvements were made and it was not qualified how much of an improvement it was, but, through the visits of the International Commission of the Red Cross and other bodies -- radio and television, that is, visitors from different media, I am saying that all this has distributed to the position of the prisoners as an act of democratic behaviour towards these people, so I believe that this comment is something usual, something that is not out of the ordinary, so that this was not a prison any more from which the outside world, the media and the international organisations were kept, because we do have cases in 1992, different camps about which different people did not know and certain persons were executed there, whereas here people were already receiving food from home. So, you cannot compare these two. So, such a comment is, to me, quite in place and even though it is not supported by any document, but if the media could visit, if the international organisations could visit, if they could influence the conditions there, then I think this comment is very much in place. Unfortunately, I did not quote this document and I did not enclose it, because I did not feel it necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you have got it then, professor, the document that you relied on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, but the professor already answered this question whether he did have this report or not. He did say that he did not have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He said he did not have it. He relied on various comments in the media and reports of the commissions and other organisations, which he did not himself read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then he says, the very last words, and it is appearing on the screen now: "Unfortunately, I did not quote this document and I did not enclose it, because I did not feel it necessary." That seems to be in somewhat contradiction to what he said earlier. I am asking him where it is. May I put the question to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may. But I think it will merely mean he is referring to so many newspaper reports and visits by the other persons, which he got to read about, and on which he formed his opinion. I am not sure he really had any particular document on which he relied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Findings of the International Committee of the Red Cross would be very important, your Honour, and the witness does say that, according to the findings of the ICRC and other organisations some other measures were undertaken, et cetera. I am asking him, did he rely on it, did he see it. He said "no", and then he said, "I did not include it." I respectfully submit that I should be entitled to pursue this to find out what the position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Find out. Let us know exactly what you did not enclose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simply because I did not find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are back to the position now where you are saying you never had it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you did have media reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Presumably, you relied on them, because you have made a finding in your report, have you not -- you have expressed an opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You would agree with me, would you not, professor, that it is very important what the ICRC found when they visited Celebici during the period 1992 -- that is a very important matter, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, am I now to assume that there are some very important sources that you relied on which are not included in your appendix?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection. He did not say that. He said he did not see the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may deal with the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not agree that I failed to include many important and relevant documents. What I said is that I used the sources that were -- to which I had access during my research. I did not have an opportunity to see it, but I was following the efforts which were made in Konjic by the organised authorities, which took care that the prisoners in Celebici were treated fairly, and what I found is that the presidency found -- that the presidency attempted to find blankets for Celebici, and that the conditions would be created for the prisoners getting medical care in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, I know, you have said all that. All I am asking you about is something that the ICRC said, which is an independent, international organisation that visited the camp and you have referred to it. The only thing that interests me is the material on which you relied in order to make the comments and express the opinion that you did. If you can find that material --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I notice that Mr. O'Sullivan is objecting. I am somewhat confused as to who in fact this witness is -- whether it is Mr.s Residovic's or Mr. O'Sullivan's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not sure he is objecting to asking questions. If a question is asked, the witness, if he is unable to answer it, the court will know what to do. I think the witness will be able to answer such a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We have been through this already once and we have the answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What I remember the witness saying is he has not read the document himself, but he got reports from media and other sources, but that is not the question being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. Professor, can you make available these media reports that you relied upon so that we can all see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have it here with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That does not matter. If you can make it available to us after you go back to Sarajevo, that would be fine. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, in your report, you make the point that, when the war started, the existing laws could not always be followed and you instance a particular example of persons being detained for longer than three days before they were brought to the court. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am just asking you if you remember saying it in your report. Maybe you do not remember saying it. If you do not, let me know and I will take you to where you said it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall, but if you could point me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means, professor. There is the chapter or section on Celebici prison, which is number 9, and I think it is the 8th paragraph -- that is my English version, but assuming the paragraph order is the same, and the paragraph starts: "According to the regulations being in effect at the time -- "

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- "at the time of these events the persons were detained and kept in detention for only three days" -- yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also make the point -- I am not dealing specifically with this -- I am using these as instances -- you also make the point than when laws were enacted or changed, it often took a significant time for the new laws to be distributed and sometimes even longer for those laws to be implemented. Do you remember expressing that opinion in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is an opinion based on the reports issued by the official gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is true. However, there are certain oscillations in that regard. Firstly, you have what we spoke of yesterday. There was a document about the appointment of the staff, that is, there were instructions already, so that on 17 April they established the Territorial Defence and they proposed -- what I am doing here is I am illustrating the events or developments that occurred because of unavailable copies of the official gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I think we understand that. I mean, please feel free to give us whatever explanation you feel appropriate, but, really, I am only asking for "Yes" or "No" answers. If you feel it is useful to go into a greater explanation, you can. I am asking you some general questions which are whether or not you said so in your report -- that is all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to explain this issue, because it is a significant one. What it is about is that, in Konjic, there was only a police prison -- not an investigative prison, which was in Mostar, so that all the detained persons who were to be investigated were allowed to be kept there for a period of time. However, the district court, in which jurisdiction the investigations were, was not operative, so it was not safe to transport 200 people there. The same in Zenica and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? We have all read your report and a very fine report it was, too. Everything you are saying now is something we have seen in it. I am not asking you to recite the report for me again. I just want you to acknowledge whether these are things that you are saying in the report. So, really, you do not have to go into all this detail. We appreciate that you have said it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but these are all things in my report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. You also make the point that communication with Sarajevo was difficult; do you remember making that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, professor, if you put all these sort of instances together -- the fact that people were detained longer than was permissible by law, and you have given us an explanation for that; the fact that laws that were enacted could not be implemented; that communication was difficult with Sarajevo at the time, and one can fully understand that in view of the siege, you would agree with me that these difficulties made Konjic a much more autonomous municipality than normally would be the case, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that it had a major influence, because I said that there were certain channels that were used by the military, and that a certain amount of communication did exist. The problem at that time was that it was not always possible to react in a timely way. Also, because the official gazette was not always printed on time, there were shortages of paper, the personnel, the staff was reduced, so there was a whole range of problems. However, in the investigation that I conducted and, also, based -- on the basis of certain decisions of the presidency here, it is clear that the Konjic municipality did not sort of strike out on its own and did things on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Please do not get me wrong --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I analysed about 110 laws that were passed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are saying that those factors did not isolate Konjic municipality -- they were still not isolated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 110 laws, which were adopted from the previous period, from the previous legislation, and they were adopted as still in force. I think that another 100 orders were also issued with the force of law and they were about different areas of life, including the humanitarian law provisions, et cetera, so, in that respect, Konjic was not cut off and isolated, including, for instance, provisions on international law regarding war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases. Professor, I really do ask you to concentrate closely on my question and give me as concise an answer as possible, just so that we can move on a little quicker. You stated in your testimony yesterday that, in Konjic, after the municipal assembly ceased to function, a crisis staff was created; do you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, can you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that the witness never stated that -- at least I never heard this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I heard it with clarity and it could be in the transcript. I am sorry I interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I may have been wrong but in my language I never heard this -- I heard war presidency, not crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will clarify it now. Is it not true yesterday, when you were testifying, you said that, in Konjic, after the municipal assembly ceased to function, there was a crisis staff and then there was a war presidency -- you said that yesterday, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The crisis staff was set out in the provisions of law, and I think you will have an opportunity to ask the people who were part of this crisis staff and I believe that the Trial Chamber will have an opportunity to hear from these persons directly. So, this crisis staff was provided by law and I do not know about its connection to the war presidency, because the war presidency was established in a situation of the immediate threat of war. That is the basis for establishing --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We seem to have a lot of difficulty communicating. It may be the translation process. I think the question I asked you was whether you said that yesterday. I did not ask you whether or not -- I did not ask you to go into an explanation. I just wanted to know whether you said yesterday that a crisis staff was created after the municipal assembly ceased to exist -- that is all I asked. Did you say it or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, I did not say that in that sense. I did not say it in the sense that -- the crisis staff has nothing to do with a session of the 17th -- that was the 9th session -- this was the last session of the municipal assembly in peacetime. The crisis staff was not formed before then and it did not exist before the 17th. The crisis staffs were established in the conditions when there was an extraordinary situation, so the crisis staff had no role here as regards the presidency or the municipal assembly which operates in the wartime conditions when the assembly is unable to meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will get the transcript during the break professor. In that way, it will be clear for everyone. Professor, you did tell us just a moment ago that the creation of a crisis staff was based in law. Can you tell us what that law is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that right now. I would have to look into the Statute of the Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think we are about to have an adjournment, so perhaps that could be another matter that you might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it is convenient for us to stop here and reassemble at 12 noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue, and kindly remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I take note of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, before the break, you said that you would look for me for some documents. Did you manage to find the document that you called D22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document D22, the one that you quoted in English, I did look at it and it has been translated, but it has not been included in this folder. Instead, there is a document relevant to the formation of a commission for the investigation of war crimes, instead of the document that you quoted it has not been included here, or it has been translated by mistake or for some other reasons, I do not know. Secondly, as far as the crisis staff is concerned, that was the other question that I owe an explanation for, I did mention the crisis staff -- it was envisaged in the regulations before the war and those regulations ceased to be in effect when an immediate threat of war was proclaimed on 17 April, when the presidency of the assembly was formed to operate under wartime conditions, or, in other words, the war presidency. Until then, the crisis staff had been envisaged, but, with the new regulations, the crisis staff was not envisaged, but, rather, the war presidency, and that is how I came to mention it as being part of previous regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will come back to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question I owe you an answer to regarding the Red Cross report, I said that I had not seen it, but I remembered watching a TV report from the Celebici prison when doctors were interviewed after the visit of a Red Cross commission and, as I promised I would send it to you, if you need it and if you want it, I can send it to you from Sarajevo to your address, a TV feature in which you see people saying that things are improving in the Celebici prison and this is said by the doctors working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just going back to that document D22 that you have explained now, the position, is that a document that you relied on, or was it something that you have seen but was of no merit in terms of your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said it is not in your appendices, professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: D22 is marked here with a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, just listen to my question, and I think it might save a lot of time if you really just listened to what I am saying. I am not challenging what you are saying. All I am asking you is for information. All I am asking you is that the document mentioned in the index to appendix D, which is referred to as D22, which you explained, quite reasonably, that was not included, by mistake -- it was an error -- all I am asking you is whether it is a document that you relied on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, that is all I wanted to know. Going to the question of the crisis -- your Honours, I am referring to page 10,209 of the transcript, lines 16 -- just dealing with the crisis staff for a moment before we move on, it is true that yesterday you said that, prior to the establishment of the war presidency, a crisis staff existed for a short while -- you did say that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe that is what I said, but, in the regulations that were in force until then envisaged a crisis staff, but, after the 17th of April those regulations ceased to be valid and a new regulation came into force on 17 April 1992. Therefore, if it existed, it could have existed for a short time and in emergency conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Precisely. If it existed, it would have existed in contravention of the regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is a question following up the answers given yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, and today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And today, a continuation of the questions. If there was a new regulation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am -- what was happening was a change of regulations -- new regulations came into force and they became effective immediately. Those regulations did not provide for a crisis staff but for a war presidency, which took the place of the presidency of the municipal assembly, and it is no longer called a crisis staff nor is such a body formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The question that I am asking you is that, whilst that may indeed be the law -- I am not challenging that for one minute -- what I am asking you is would you agree with me that, if a crisis staff continued to exist in Konjic after 17 April, for a short time, that that crisis staff would be contrary to the regulations which required the establishment of a war presidency -- that is all I am asking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that. I did not say that, after 17 April -- I said that, according to the regulations, it could have existed until 17 April, but not after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What the question is: if it actually did, is it not contrary to the former regulations -- that is all -- not that you said so, but, if it did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it exists after, but it does not exist after the 17th when the new regulations came into effect. It could have existed until the 17th, but not after the 17th, when the new regulations came into force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that is your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that you are absolutely certain, beyond any question of doubt, that, come 17 April 1992, in Konjic there definitely did not exist a crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. You indicated yesterday that the practice of having the municipal assembly stopped at the same time -- sorry, the practice of sitting, the municipal assembly sitting, stopped at the same time as the Territorial Defence was transformed into the Bosnian army; do you remember saying that, or words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember saying that in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I have not fairly quoted it to you in the way that you did say it. Did you say something like that, and if so, tell us what you did say? A.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have an objection. The question should be clear. The question is rather unusual for a cross-examination. The witness does not know what to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You frame it unambiguously -- let us hear what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will try again. The practice of the municipal assembly, sitting as a municipal assembly, did that stop or cease at the same time that the Territorial Defence was transformed into what became the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions for the cessation of sittings by the municipal assembly are conditions of war, which make it impossible for deputies in the municipality to meet and sit in the assembly. In that case, those sittings are not practised, because it is not possible for them to gather, except by exposing them to great risk, or under no circumstances at all, but it is not said anywhere that they cannot meet. If conditions exist they may, but the town was surrounded, and only some people could come -- some people had already left, others had gone somewhere, so the conditions were not normal for the municipal assembly to function, and that is why the law envisaged the formation of a presidency of the assembly, the task of which is to substitute the assembly and, when the municipal assembly meets again, it has to approve all the decisions taken in the meantime. Therefore, the presidency meets when the assembly cannot meet, and, in Konjic, after 17 April, it really could not meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, professor. I did not really ask you all that, but, never mind. Professor, are you saying that the assembly in Konjic did not meet after 17 April 1992; are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, are you aware that, under the old laws governing the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia relating to those -- those laws relating to what happened concerning the governing -- I withdraw that, your Honour. Professor, are you aware that, under the old laws of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia relating to the functioning of the war presidency, that the war presidency was a military and civilian body that took over the functioning of the municipality in times of war. My question is: were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that the war presidency, this one we are talking about, was not a military body but a civilian organ of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, may I interrupt you and tell you that is not my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are referring to old regulations which do not envisage a presidency in the form in which it appeared on 17 April. I told you that, according to the old regulations, a crisis staff was envisaged, which took over in municipalities in emergency situations and the presidency is a new body which started to be applied as of the 17th, that is, after the 9th session which was the last under wartime conditions -- as from then, there is a war presidency. I am not aware, nor did I study these things particularly in the past, so that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may be that you do not know. You talked about the crisis staff. Would I be correct if I said that the crisis staff was responsible for military and civilian matters in the municipality in times of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that the territorial and the police or the MUP chiefs or commanders were part of the war presidency in Konjic during 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And are you aware that persons could be invited to become members of the war presidency during 1992 in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid I do not understand the question -- which persons? Excuse me, could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question, which may assist you. Are you aware that the war presidency had the authority and the capacity to appoint persons as members of the war presidency, if it so chose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there is a regulation about that as to who are the members of a war presidency, but the presidency could, if necessary, invite people to attend meetings, but they were not in the capacity of members of the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So just to clarify the point, what you are saying is that it lacked the authority or power to appoint persons other than those prescribed as members of the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Membership in the war presidency is stipulated by law and all the people who do not meet those requirements are not members, but they may attend meetings of the presidency, should the presidency need them to clear up something, or to come to an agreement over something, but these are two different things. In that case, such people were invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You are aware -- I withdraw that. Did the law, in relation to the war presidency, change on 20 May 1992 so far as you are aware -- was there a change to the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a change in the law, insofar as the aim was to clearly specify the composition of the war presidency, and it was stipulated that the president of the assembly, representatives of deputy clubs of the various political parties that were legally elected, representatives at the elections, and also to be included in the war presidency was the commander of the Civil Defence, the chief of the public security service, and the chief of defence of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In respect of the law that applied before 20 May 1992, in relation to the war presidency, did that law provide that the war presidency had responsibilities in both military and civilian matters, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war presidency has the competence as a civilian organ of authority to decide on civilian matters and questions of defence or, rather, preparations for defence of the country, but it does not have the competence to issue orders and control and command military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The law of 20 May 1992, are you aware that, in some municipalities -- indeed, in many -- this law was not implemented for a considerable period of time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you will be having a military expert here, and an expert report, it is my view that it is up to the competence of that expert to explain and talk about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not asking you so much a military question, professor; I am asking you about the implementation of the law of 20 May 1992 relating to the war presidency, which you have spoken of at length -- a simple question -- was there a delay in its implementation in a number of municipalities? It is not a question which is exclusively in the domain of an expert on military matters, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The presidency continues to do its work. This law did not affect the duties and obligations of the war presidency. It is a law on the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Let me put the question more directly. Are you aware that the law of 20 May 1992 was not in fact implemented in Konjic until October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, professor, would you take your binder of documents and go to D19? Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The first part of that document is a letter, which has an attachment -- it is the attachment that interests me. Can you find the attachment there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the first page of the text after the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, in my English version, it is 354, but I do not know what it is in yours. In that document, 349 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What does the decision there represent?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What does that decision represent to you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The presidency of the municipal assembly of Konjic," then it enumerates the members of the presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that not the implementation of the law of 20 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot see -- it is not very legible what they are referring to here. Could we please look in the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot see the preamble here. I cannot read it, because it is a bad copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, I am not sure how this managed to be translated in view of that, but I will read to you what I have in my English version of the preamble and any part else that you have difficulty reading. It reads: "Pursuant to article -- " Then there is some doubt as to the number, but it would appear to have a 40 in it: " -- of the decree with the force of law of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on defence, official gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina number 4/92, the presidency of the municipality of Konjic, functioning as and with the powers of the assembly, at its session on 26 October 1992 hereby renders a decision." Can you read from there on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I can read on, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not want you to read it out; I just want you to look at the document and tell me whether or not this document represents a record of the implementation of the law of 20 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That does not mean that the war presidency did not work. I said, and I still assert that the war presidency sat as of 17 April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: All I am asking you is whether the law of 20 May was implemented and whether this document was the implementation of the 20 May law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But the documents --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: -- show that the war presidency had come into existence much earlier -- even the order appointing Mr. Delalic as coordinator, if you look at the heading, it says "War Presidency".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is true. I am not suggesting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said the presidency probably existed, although there is an order of October 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The point I am trying to make is that the actual implementation at law did not take place until October 1992 -- that is the only point I am trying to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The war presidency existed even before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may well have existed and we do not argue that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: His own document shows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the only point I try to make. You are aware during May and June that the head of the Territorial Defence in Konjic changed some five or six times -- are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean is this in my report? Where did I mention it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am just asking you whether you are aware of that. You may not be aware of it -- which is fine, just tell us, but I am asking you, were you aware that, during May and June, the head of the Territorial Defence in Konjic changed some five or six times? You may not be aware of it -- no problem if you are not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not like to answer that question, because it is part of the expertise of the military expert. He followed these changes and he knows about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Fine. I will ask you another question. Do you know who appointed -- sorry, I withdraw that. Did you know that it was the war presidency who appointed the heads of the TO, or the command of the TO during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. The war presidency proposed, on 17 April, a commander of the Territorial Defence and the appointment was approved by the supreme command according to the law that you mentioned. Later it changed so that the presidency would no longer propose it, but the commander of the Territorial Defence would be appointed by the supreme command -- not the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you do know that there were changes, but you did not know how many -- is that what I am to assume from your answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, what I know is what was in regulations. I do not know whether people were sick or wounded or otherwise indisposed and were replaced. That, I did not follow. That would be part of the expertise of the military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Let us ask you something that you have just mentioned, so presumably it is in your military expertise. You said that these changes were approved in Sarajevo by the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- head of the military in Sarajevo. Did you ever sight any document that showed the approval of these recommendations or appointments from Sarajevo or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, you are asking these things of me now. I did not deal with this issue, and I did not follow these changes in the Territorial Defence, because this is part of the military expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. So, so far as you are concerned then, your position on this is (a), you do not know whether anyone was appointed and (b), if they were appointed by the war presidency, you do not know whether or not that was approved in Sarajevo -- all you know is that that is something that should have happened, according to your understanding of the regulations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not my opinion. The war presidency could not appoint the commander of the Territorial Defence, that is number 1. Number 2, if they changed frequently, then the question is what was the form of the order which was given to Konjic. In principle, the war presidency cannot appoint the commander of the Territorial Defence. This person is appointed by the supreme command, because the presidency is a civilian body and they cannot appoint military commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not quarrelling with you for one moment on that. I am really trying to find out whether you yourself know, by looking at material or documents, whether you sighted any evidence that Sarajevo -- when I say "Sarajevo", I mean the headquarters of military command, or whoever the body was responsible -- actually approved the proposal by the war presidency to appoint Territorial Defence commanders -- that is all I am asking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
