utterances.text: For the third time I am telling you that I did not research these documents and it was not a matter of my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tell us, professor, how is it then that yesterday you were able to say that, when the municipal authorities ceased to appoint the commanders of the Territorial Defence in Konjic, you stated that, when you were asked that question, you said, "They stopped appointing the command of the Territorial Defence when the old Territorial Defence ceased to exist and the new Territorial Defence was established." How did you come to that opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because, when the commander of the Territorial Defence was appointed on 17 April, he was proposed by the presidency -- that means not appointed, just proposed -- and the assembly voted on it and the approval came from Sarajevo, from the command of the staff of Territorial Defence, that is, the republican staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And is that included in your documents, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was also pointed out in the records of the sitting of 17 April, that this was a selection that has to be approved by the command in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you take us to that, please, and show us where it is that you say that exists in your attached materials and just draw our attention to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pause). The record of the session of the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is D what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps to help you, could I take you to the paragraph immediately ahead of item 1, which, if your Honours please, is at page -- it is the back of page 307 -- it is the centre of the page and it is page 4 of the report. If you go there, you can see a reference to the Territorial Defence -- do you see that immediately above item 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you just please give me a reference to the page of my report?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I think our best position is to take you to the document. You mentioned the document. The only one I could find when I studied your material that was relevant was the document numbered D8, and it is the minutes of the meeting of the assembly on 17 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The only reference I could find to the Territorial Defence was immediately above item 1, which is on page 4 of the English version of it, but item 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is on page 2 in my version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, unless there is some difficulty with the translation, I had -- I will just ask the question -- I had some difficulty finding there a reference to that appointment being approved by Sarajevo, as you said just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This election was not valid until it was approved by Sarajevo. In fact, these elections were confirmed by the higher command in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: All I am asking, professor, is please show us that document where that was confirmed in Sarajevo -- that is the only thing I am asking. Please take us to that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see this document. The document which arrived from Sarajevo, I do not know in which way it was sent from Sarajevo. It was a wartime situation. If it existed, it will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You do not even know that it exists, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I said clearly that I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, in your opinion, if it did not exist, and it never existed, then this appointment, according to your view, is illegal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would not be according to the regulations. Appointments had to be approved by Sarajevo -- that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, seeing as we are looking at copies of minutes of war presidency meetings, where did you obtain these minutes from? I think I misspoke -- I said "war presidency meetings", I think it would be more correct to ask where did you obtain the minutes of the municipal assembly of 17 April 1992 -- where did you obtain them from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I received it through the Defence counsel's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you also made reference and included copies of minutes of the war presidency meetings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you get those from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were the minutes of 3 June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What D number is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is on 18 May, the war presidency, and there is another one from 3 June, from the session of the presidency held on 3 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you attempt to locate any minutes of the war presidency yourself, or did you just rely on that which was given to you by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two sources for these documents. One is the Institute for Investigation of the War Crimes and what I was given by the office of the Defence counsel, so, whatever they had, I received and whatever they did not have -- I simply --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I simply did not have access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the Konjic municipality has no record of these minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you approach the Konjic municipality at all for these records?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not receive the record -- I already had it in Sarajevo, so I did not have a need to look for it specifically, this particular one, and I did not receive any other records.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that because they told you they did not have it, or is it because you just did not pursue it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what the reason is, but I did not receive the records, and so I did not look into them, provided they exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from the minutes particularly, say, of the war presidency that you have included in your report, did you have access to any other minutes of the war presidency of the Konjic municipality during 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, with the exception of what I have included here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that your position is this -- and it is something that is important, so I really need to make sure that I have it right -- are you saying that the war presidency was a civilian institution with no authority over the Territorial Defence or the headquarters of the Bosnian army -- is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It cannot control and command the Territorial Defence and the military, that is what I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, if a person, who you would expect to be familiar with the events in Konjic at that time, said that the war presidency was in charge of both the civilian and defence matters --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, your Honours, to this form of questioning. It is whatever another person may say here before this Trial Chamber, but it is not appropriate to ask the witness that question in this form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may well depend very much on who it was who said it rather than anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are comparing what he would say as against what somebody else had said -- you can ask him your questions in the way he could answer it himself, whether or not he agrees with that view. He is an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As an expert, professor, would you disagree with a person who would be expected to be familiar with the actual events that occurred in the Konjic municipality at that time and I am talking about 1992, if he said that the war presidency was in charge of both the civilian and defence matters, at least as far as the municipality went -- you would disagree with that, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I answered that question yesterday. I said that the war presidency and the municipal assembly engaged in military matters only insofar as it prepares for the defence of the municipality and that means that it provides the conditions for defence and that is separate from the issues of control and command of the units. There, the war presidency have no role, but, as far as the preparations, it has a constitutional role, in a sense to provide financial materiel and other conditions and that is the duty of the assembly and the war presidency, and so this is provided in the law, to prepare for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If that same person, who one would expect to have some knowledge of these matters, was then asked, if the war presidency had any authority to direct the actions of the territorial staff, including its commander, and that that person answered "yes, but not the exclusive authority", you would disagree with that, too, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You would not agree with it -- what is your position -- do you agree that the war presidency had the authority, at least in part, to direct the actions of the territorial staff, including Territorial Defence, including its commander -- do you agree with that statement, or do you disagree with it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Again, the question is not clear, and the witness did answer parts of this question on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I may persist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Be a little more precise as to what is exactly true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What I am saying to you is this: we are speaking of a person who, one would assume, would know something about what was happening in relation to military matters, the war presidency, and the Territorial Defence in Konjic in 1992. All I am asking you is: if that person were to say that the war presidency had the authority, in part, to direct the actions of the territorial staff, including its commander, would you agree with that as a statement, or would you say that that statement is wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not agree with that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, when the Defence gave you all the documents -- the Defence for Mr. Delalic gave you all the documents to review for the purposes of your report, did they give you a copy of his interview conducted between the Office of the Prosecutor and him in the presence of his counsel on 22 March 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Who are you referring to -- who is the "him"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only state that, if this happened, this was not in accordance with the regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is not the question -- whether the interview which he had was part of the briefing which was given to you by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you disagree with what Mr. Delalic said in his record of interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In what respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In respect of the question relating to the fact that the war presidency had authority, in part, to direct the actions of the territorial staff, including that of its commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The witness already said that he did not agree with such a statement. I do not understand why this question is now being repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am merely following His Honour's request for clarification, so your objection is not to me but to His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has clearly stated he did not agree with that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If that is a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In fact both statements can be true, because during war civil functions and military functions get mixed, as one of the expert witnesses said here, so maybe he is also right and he is also right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We are dealing with opinions here. The Trial Chamber will now rise and resume at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you may proceed with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, immediately before the adjournment for lunch, I made a mistake and I want to correct it and give you an opportunity to respond if necessary. I said it was in a record of interview of Mr. Delalic of 22 March 1996. On reviewing the matter over lunch I made a mistake -- it was in fact 22 August 1996, I apologise for that. Does that date make any difference to the answer that you gave at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, you recall we were talking about the powers of the war presidency and its powers to appoint and matters of that nature, particularly concerning military matters; do you remember we discussed that? Yesterday, and I am referring to page 10,221 of the transcript, lines 15 to 22, Madam Residovic asked you some questions about the war presidency and she asked you whether the war presidency could have appointed Zejnil Delalic to any military position, and your answer to that: "No, it could not have done so, because the military authorities would make such appointments." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you review any documentation, either supplied to you by the Defence or other material which was signed or appeared to be signed by the accused, Mr. Delalic, at the relevant time in which he appears to be performing any of his duties, and I refer to the period of time when he was a coordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these documents that were given to you by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember who gave them to me. I only have the documents about Zejnil Delalic which I received from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you include all of those in your binder of materials, or did you leave some of them out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not include all of them, because I read quite a number regarding the interrogation and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If any of them related to the performance of military functions and duties, would you have included those if you had seen them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not, because that belongs to the military expertise. The documents referring to Zejnil Delalic in any military capacity are probably somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. Your Honours, might these documents or group of documents be marked for identification and one copy shown to the witness, please, your Honour. There is a copy for your Honours and copies for the Defence. A copy of these has previously been given to the Defence, your Honour. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor document number 210, 211, 212 and 213.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The first document that I -- just look through them for the moment and perhaps copies can be given to their Honours, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, these documents have not been tendered by the Prosecutor so far, so I am wondering what are the grounds for the use of these documents for an expert witness on historical issues. Of course, we object to the use of such documents with this type of witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, what is your --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: May I continue? Professor, have you seen these documents before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These are similar, are they not, to the other type of documents that you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, your Honours. The witness has said that he never saw these documents before. I do not know how it is possible to proceed with new questions on the basis of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, do these documents appear to be regular documents and the sort of documents that you saw yesterday and said that they are the type of documents that an historian would ordinarily rely upon and similar to the sorts of documents that you yourself in fact relied upon when you compiled your report -- that is right, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are documents of a military nature and I did not make any assessment regarding relations in the army, except for those having to do with the war presidency, and its powers, and the defence forces of Konjic. Therefore, on each of these documents, there is a signature, and all the relevant indicators, I would not be so bold as to make any conclusions about them, because I never saw them before and I have not analysed or studied them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course, and I am not asking you to do that. What I am asking you to do is to tell me whether they have the same kind of indicia of reliability on them, namely, the stamps, the signatures, the dates, the actual contents, that you relied on in all the other documents that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And as an historian, you would satisfy yourself of those matters, rely on these, too, for that purpose, if you were asked to express an opinion on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, this is the sort of material that historians would traditionally rely upon for this purpose, would they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dealing with the Celebici prison itself, again yesterday in the transcript Madam Residovic asked you about Celebici prison and I am referring, your Honours, to page 10,229, lines 4 to 17. Madam Residovic asked you: "Did your research lead you to conclude anything about the kind of prison that Celebici was" and then she asked you, "was it a civilian or military prison?" And in fairness to you, you said, "To tell you the truth, I am not an expert on prisons" so I think we need to start on that basis, but then you did go on and you said: "But I was not able to establish it -- I think there are several agencies that had competence over that prison, so it was very difficult to establish." Then you said for a time it was a civilian prison and then a military one and then you said it came under the control of the police, the army and then the higher court and so forth -- you made those observations. Again, professor, did you study documentation made available to you by the Defence in relation to the Celebici prison in order to determine what type of prison it was and who had control over it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first place, I did not find a single document on the establishment of the prison. I assume that the first prisoners in Celebici were prisoners who were in police custody and that they could have been transferred to the Celebici prison after 20 April, when that facility was taken over by the Yugoslavia army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably then, the police did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the Defence make available to you any documents from the State Commission for the Exchange of War Prisoners -- were any documents from that body made available to you so that you could consider it when you wrote your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not study those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ask that this document be marked for identification, a copy for all parties, including their Honours and might one copy be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has not actually identified it himself. He merely says they are like other documents which he has dealt with -- not this particular one. What is he identifying it for?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is another document. I am asking for it to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A new one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor document number 214.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, could you quietly, to yourself, read through that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that before, professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you think it may have assisted you with that issue of determining what sort of prison the Celebici prison was during a particular time of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard to tell on the basis of one reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ad hoc. One would need to really carry out a proper analysis. It is not possible to state, offhand, what I would have done if I had it. I would have probably taken it into consideration, read it carefully and analysed it, but this document would have to be verified, it would have to be checked. I would not accept it before checking it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand that, and of course it would be unfair of me to ask you now to opine on the matter on just one very short reading of it, but, professor, putting that aside, do you notice that there is an archive reference to the top of that document -- it is hand-written, I believe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "State Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And then, immediately beneath that, there appears to be a reference by a machine and then immediately below that there is a hand-written reference, is there not, and that is an archive reference -- am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was entered subsequently. It states that it is a document of the State Commission for Exchange of Prisoners, and then in handwriting is added the number of the register -- the register number and the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It appears to be a telex message, does it not, a typewritten telex message -- the sort one might expect to be sent from one place to another by electronic means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I am not getting the interpretation into Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was saying it appears to be the sort of document that is sent by means of electronic telex from one centre to another, does it not -- it appears to be like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It appears to be a document that was directed from Konjic to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it is the sort of document that you would expect to see, would you not, as an historian, researching into this area, having regard to the events of the time, its contents, the date of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is nothing about it that looks terribly suspicious, is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it does not. With verification of its contents, this document would probably be acceptable as authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, professor, if it had been given to you by Mr.s Residovic, would you have accepted it like this, or what would you have done in order to check its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Any document that may point to the truth, I would verify, and I would accept it if I would be able to confirm its reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, I know that you are probably getting tired and I am getting close to the end of my cross-examination, you will probably be happy to know, but there are a few more questions that I would like to ask you, if I can. Do you remember, we had some discussion about you looking at documents from international agencies and, in particular, I asked you some questions about the International Committee of the Red Cross -- do you remember me asking you questions about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I think, yesterday, you said in your evidence-in-chief that you had seen the Bassiouni report on the commission of experts in relation to prisons and you found it to be a credible and reliable document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you happen to look at any other documents which were generated by international agencies or non-government organisations in relation to perhaps not only Celebici prison but other prisons that were available from the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I looked at the documents that are used -- that have been used in certain international conferences on events in Bosnia and they mostly talk about camps and ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you include any or all of those with your papers, the attachments to your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, no, I did not, except for the material that relates directly to Konjic, and the report of the Bassiouni commission was part of the basis on which I formed my opinions in this report. I think that it is fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I ask your Honours the following document be marked for identification and a copy shown to the witness. This is a long document and I want you to glance through it because it is only the last page I want to ask you about, in particular. (Handed). I include all of it for its completeness. Might it be given the next number in order, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor document 215.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might glance through it, professor, but it is the last page I want to go to. (Pause). Professor, this document that you now have in front of you, this purports to be a report, does it not, from the Secretariat of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe and it is dated Prague, 10 September 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In particular, on the very last page, which in the English version, your Honours, is page 5 and it is the back of page 4, there is a reference there, is there not, to Konjic, Celebici; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, let me turn to that page. Yes, on page 4, Konjic and Celebici are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, professor, have you seen this report before -- was it made available to you by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I have not seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, professor, just looking at it -- and I know it is hard of me to ask you to express too far an opinion on it, but does it appear to be the sort of document that you would rely upon as an historian if you had to write about the events that occurred during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it contains the sort of indicia of reliability that professional historians like yourself would accept as being an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, in relation to the documents that were in fact given to you by the Defence, did you carry out verification checks, on all of them, or just in relation to some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In cases where I could verify, I did so, either on the spot, or by analysing the authenticity of the document subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did you do in those cases where you could not verify them -- there was neither the means, the time or whatever, what did you do in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The things that I was unable to verify, I did not include here. I think that all the documents that are included here, with the exception of the last one, which I mentioned, which did not have the proper characteristics that I could rely on, I think that I spoke about those yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Included among the material that was provided to you by the Defence, did you see any media material, be it videos, newspapers, and the like in relation to the accused, Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw a videotape about the opening of a railroad line and I saw Zejnil Delalic there -- it was a celebration of opening the railroad line, the train went from Pazaric to Jablanica. That was a very big event for Konjic during the war and also for all communities between Pazaric and Jablanica. I saw some other footage as well, but not those which included Mr. Delalic, but I did review a lot of footage that relates to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see any videotapes of him dressed in military uniforms and participating in television interviews -- anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think I saw him wearing a military uniform, but I did not see others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him addressing troops -- a video --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That was not part of my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that you told us yesterday that, in relation to those documents which are in the nature of certificates that had been provided to Madam Residovic, the Defence, from a number of institutions, but including I think the Konjic municipality, that you relied on those certificates in order to express your opinion; do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I relied on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you told at any stage that on at least two occasions these sorts of documents that have been provided turned out to be false -- I am talking about documents provided by the Konjic municipality -- did anyone ever tell you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think your position --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honours, I am not aware of the fact that we have identified any falsified documents from the Konjic municipality during the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a matter that we can advise Madam Residovic on, and I take it from her what she is saying is she did not know and I accept if she did not know she could not have told him, but we have been informed on two occasions that two certificates issued by the Konjic municipality were false. If Madam Residovic says she did not know that, I accept that and I accept that this witness could not have been told that if she did not know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you been able to inform the Defence about such an experience?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We were informed by the Defence -- in fact, my colleague Ms. McHenry was informed by the Defence. She knows the details of it. I will ask her to address the court on it when I have finished my cross-examination. I think, professor, your position on all of this is that the view you express on the prison, on the role of the coordinator, on the functions and responsibilities of the war presidency, and such matters that you have written of in your report are all based on the material that you saw, and that that view holds, so long as you are not presented with any contra material -- is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that, I am just asking you if you agree that you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that, in my field of expertise, we have a rule that you write a text based on the material that you have available and that such a piece of writing is good until new discoveries are found. The process never ends and that is at least the case in my profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed, professor. That concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, given the length of the cross-examination, I would like to ask for a brief recess so that I can organise my notes and then ask questions in re-examination and then address you on other matters and tender documents for admission. I think, your Honours, that I am entitled to this, because the Prosecutor offered completely new documents during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I want to find out --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: At the end of this document you just presented, the word written is "Belalic" -- is it a typographical error or is just one you received from the Bosnian Government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no explanation as to why it is "Belalic" rather than Delalic. I can only assume that some typographical error was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You cannot make an assumption in a criminal trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was not suggesting that. That is as the document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Because I thought while making copies for us you might have made a typographical error.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, we did not. This is the document as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is "Belalic" also a name common in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, such a name does exist, and this document with the identical name was provided to the Defence by the Prosecutor about two years ago, and so the references to this name have nothing to do with my client. It states nothing but "Mr. Belalic".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Belalic is a name in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is a possible name in Bosnia -- it is not as common as Delalic, but it does exist, because the name of Delalic exists in many areas -- in Sandzak in eastern Bosnia, in Sarajevo and elsewhere and Belalic is a name, but I do not know how widespread it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr.s Residovic, in any event we would be having a break at about 4 o'clock. So, we will continue, but I do not know how long you really think you would need merely to re-examine your witness. How long do you think you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that I will not need a lengthy period of time, but given that we just received 10 new documents, I would need about an hour to review them in the light of the entire testimony and then maybe in a very short period of time I could be able to re-examine the witness -- maybe I would need no more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would just like for the record to indicate that we disclosed these documents to Madam Residovic the moment we got them, which was recently, I admit, but she certainly has them, so it is not as though she has never seen them before, and certainly one of them she has had for a very long time. If there is any suggestion that she never saw them before, then either she does not read her mail or she is not exactly stating the position as it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not say that I never saw them -- I said that I had one of them for two years, but I said that they were offered today for the first time with respect to this witness and this is why I would like to review them in the light of the entire testimony, and I would need no more than one hour, and then, within 15 minutes, I will be able to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it should be possible for you to start your re-examination at 4 o'clock. We will come back here at 4 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (A short break).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours. If I might while Mr.s Residovic is getting settled, Mr. Niemann has asked me to clarify a matter that was raised previously, which is that on two separate occasions the Prosecution has been given from the Defence certificates from officials in the Konjic municipality about what was in the records and the certificates turned out to be false. We are not suggesting for one second that Defence counsel knew about it -- in fact, on one of those occasions it was Defence counsel who first came to us and said he had already discovered the information was incorrect and we should not rely on them. I just wanted to clarify that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May it please the court, thank you. Before I start with my questions, I should like the witness to be shown again Prosecutor's Exhibit 215. (Handed). Professor, would you please look at that document once again? Will you tell me, please, professor, whether it says on your copy that it is a translation of a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, is there a seal, a signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you see on this document a source for this report of the Secretariat of the Conference for European Cooperation and Security -- a book, a text book, or any publisher that would indicate the source of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you, professor, to be kind enough to turn to the one but last page of this document. In the translation it is page 60 and the last paragraph -- let us make sure we are looking at the same one -- it starts with "it is not clear" -- is that what you are looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to read that sentence, professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "It is not clear which local authority is competent for these two areas, the Croatian Defence Council or the Muslim armed forces. However, the area is being supervised by Muslim policemen."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, professor. I would now like to ask you to turn to page 42 of this translation. It is the continuation of a list of detention centres. At the top of that page, do you see the number 20?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell me whether, on your copy, after number 20, it is stated, "Konjic, Celebici, oil warehouse"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the third line, which according to the beginning of this list is an indication of the authority in charge of that detention centre. Does it say in the third line, from what we have just said, that is, "Konjic, Celebici" -- does it say the competent authority is Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, if you as an historian take into account these two facts indicated in the same report, is there a serious contradiction between the statement on page 60 and this statement on page 42?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, for you as an historian, does such a contradiction in a document detract from the value of the document in terms of reliability?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, let us please re-examine page 60. In the third paragraph from the bottom with the heading underlined, saying "Konjic Celebici", the one but last sentence, does it read as follows in your text: "From neutral or independent sources we have learnt that the holes in the wooden wall are indicative of its bad intentions -- evil intentions." Professor, if you were to hear the testimony of more than 15 witnesses in this court, none of whom spoke of a wooden wall and holes in that wall, would that fact provoke in you as an historian further doubts as to the validity of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in answer to questions from my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, Mr. Niemann, you recalled that you saw a videotape feature with a conversation with the doctors who were in Celebici. Will you please read the last sentence of the third paragraph from the bottom, beginning with the words "it appears"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "It appears that a small clinic with medicines was improvised merely for the sake of our visit."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If what you saw in that TV programme contained certain facts and if you were to hear the testimony of those doctors in this courtroom, and other witnesses who confirmed that this infirmary had existed throughout the time of the existence of the Celebici prison, would that fact be in contradiction with this conclusion we just read in the mentioned report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would that, professor, be an additional contradiction which would further detract from the reliability of this document for any expert in your field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in view of only a few answers that you have now given, and bearing in mind that neither you nor I have had time to fully analyse this report, could you, professor, tell me, in view of these contradictions, could such a document be a reliable basis for drawing conclusions and for making an opinion by an historian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, professor. I should now like the professor to be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 214. (Handed). Professor, a moment ago, when the Prosecutor showed you this document, you voiced your opinion about it. Allow me to ask you now whether this document contains a list -- does it contain a signature -- a signature of the person who compiled the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it customary in our country for any official document or a document issued by anybody to bear the stamp of that body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is customary.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document bear the stamp of the body which allegedly compiled this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does it contain that stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I do not wish to repeat, but you have already noticed that this document, in addition to the typed text, has some hand-written notes on it. In view of those facts, I would like to ask you, professor, whether you could tell us whether such a document would be a sufficiently reliable one for an historian and for yourself as a basis for his opinion about certain facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document, after a thorough verification, I would take into consideration, as I would any other source which needs to be verified and compared -- when we have no choice, then an historian can -- and I am now talking as an historian -- then we take into consideration even those sources which may be of assistance in establishing the truth by comparing the date it contains and establishing its reliability. This document, as well as the previous one, are seriously subject to criticism and doubts as to its contents being reliable -- one would have to adopt a critical approach, because it does not contain all the elements of an authentic or reliable source.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When my learned colleague, Mr. Moran, went through the document in your folder, you reached a document which is the statute of the cultural society in Vienna, and you said, at the time, that that document does not contain all the necessary elements and that you did not take it into consideration as a basis for your expert opinion. Professor, this document, which is now before you, is it a document of that kind of nature, that is, with such shortcomings that you could not use it for making an expert opinion regarding the facts it contains?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the end of the examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am not getting the interpretation, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the end of the examination and cross-examination and re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, I would just now like to repeat my offer regarding the tendering of evidence, if I may. But I must say that I am not hearing the Bosnian interpretation of what you are saying, and I am trying to understand you from a distance as much as I can. It is fine now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your application is to tender the evidence which you indicated at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will be more precise, your Honour. I should first like to tender into evidence the report marked as D135/1 -- the Prosecutor had no objections regarding the report yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objections, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should also like to tender into evidence the maps marked D137/1 and again the Prosecutor had no objection yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objections, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Documents D136/1 and annexes 1A to C and the Prosecutor yesterday also had no objections regarding these documents and I would also like to tender documents from the annex D with the limited purpose as documents contained in this folder but which were a valid basis for the compilation of the report and for the testimony of this witness in court. I should also like to tender for the same purpose and in the same way, and within the framework of our same requests, the three videotapes marked as D138/1, D139/1 and D140/1, which this witness said he used as a basis for his expert opinion. That is only within those frameworks, and within that meaning. Yesterday we already admitted into evidence a certain number of excerpts from those tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Within the limits of the application, has the Prosecution any objections? The Defence has spelt out the purposes for which the exhibits are being tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, firstly dealing with the videos, so long as they are being tendered in relation to the excerpts that we have seen. We were given videos which were much longer than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Only the excerpts shown in the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As long as it is only the excerpts, we have no objection. Certainly we confirm that the documents, through annex A to C, we have no objection to being tendered. Our position with respect to the documents in annex D is that, with respect to documents -- all the documents except D31 through to D39, our position on that is that we do not object to them being tendered as documents that were relied upon by the historian when he compiled his report. We have no objection to that. Our position is we do not accept that they are valid documents which an historian, duly qualified, would traditionally rely upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Defence has not made any claim outside -- it is relying on him as his expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We do not quarrel with the fact that he relied on them. We are saying if it is sought to say an historian in the profession of an historian would ordinarily rely upon such material, we would argue with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Considering even the contents themselves, there is no way he could have used it for any other purpose other than for his opinion for what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He was asked to express two opinions. One was would he rely on them and the other was would historians ordinarily rely on them. It is the second component we object to in relation to those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am going to join in moving the admission of some of these -- I think there is no evidence before the Trial Chamber that they are anything but documents which people in that profession would rely upon. That is an entire exercise we went through yesterday afternoon, and I do not think that Mr. Niemann's objection to that is founded in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not see him making any objections to any claims other than what you have said, except you extending it beyond any opinion on which the historian has founded his reports. Then perhaps that may be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think his objection was that they would be the type of documents that historians, in general, would rely upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is quite true. Let me say that against Mr. Moran's client I have no objection whatsoever to any of these documents being admitted in his case, if that is his application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He is not the one tendering them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If he seeks to tender them in his case against his client I am merely indicated we have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not sure you can break up evidence like that -- admit it in respect of one accused and exclude it in respect of the other accused. If the evidence comes, it comes as a whole and can be used against or in favour of any accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am pleased to hear that. I thought there would be considerable debate about what evidence could be used against whom, but I am delighted to hear your Honour say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In certain matters probably the argument would be valid. For example, the statement of an accused in which he implicates another accused, that can only probably be used, his own statement, against him. Then you would have to draw the distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think your application is granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, you said very well we have tendered the evidence in connection with the testimony of this witness. How future historians may deal with the documents tendered, it is up to them. I should also like to ask not only the excerpts from the tapes to be admitted, because they were admitted yesterday, but that the tapes that I showed yesterday to the professor and he said that the contents of those tapes, which he received from the Institute for War Crimes and from television, that it was also something that he used in making his conclusions and his comparisons with the other documentation he had. Therefore, for this same limited purpose, I tender all three videotapes into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: To the extent the excerpts that were shown in the court -- certain excerpts from the videos which were shown in the court, you only want those portions to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which are relevant to his opinion for the purpose for which they are being shown, I think that is all you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is what Mr. Niemann said. One video is of two hours duration. You do not want the whole of the two hours videotape to be admitted into evidence but only the portion that was shown in the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understood that you admitted those excerpts yesterday, but since some of the tapes are in English, this witness said that he had relied upon those videotapes as well, and I think that we have admitted into evidence in a similar way a large number of documents, not for the truth of the contents or for the authenticity of those videotapes, but for the purpose that he relied on them, and I think that we admitted many tapes on the basis of your ruling that we never saw -- we maybe only saw two or three minutes of them. So I think the totality of the material that this witness has offered to the court and which served as a basis for his written report should be admitted. Of course, that is for a limited purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that is the end of this witness's questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: May I respond to what Madam Residovic said? These videotapes go on for hours. She is seeking to tender the whole lot. Presumably everybody else and your Honours will have to sit down one day and listen to them all. I object to that. I have no objection to matters which are being shown in court and which the witness has commented upon at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is already in evidence and it is for the Trial Chamber to use it when it wants to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I move the admission of Prosecution Exhibits 210 to 215 as documents which the Prosecution showed to the witness for the purposes of impeachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not as substantive evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour -- at this stage, I might say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are not impeaching him -- you are just showing him certain documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You never impeached his credit at any stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are not questioning his credibility with respect to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is in a negative sense impeachment, in this sense: if there was a range of material available on a particular point, and the witness could have seen it, because the party that called him could have made it available but did not, then, in my submission, your Honour, it is not impeachment in the sense that it is not the witness's fault, but it goes to the issue of the material which was made available to the witness in order for him to express an opinion. It may well be that -- and it will be our subsequent argument -- that if the witness had seen this material, he could well have formed a different opinion. On that basis it is impeachment, in my respectful submission, and should be admitted for that limited purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you any reply to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I object to the admission into evidence of these documents tendered by the Prosecutor now, especially in view of the re-examination that I did on the basis of those documents -- the witness did not identify them, many of them cannot be a reliable source for anyone and especially not for a scholar and historian. As for the second question, may I be allowed to ask the witness just one question before I answer Mr. Niemann -- may I do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think you can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Your Honour, I object of course to this second submission, because we have also heard a distinguished professor of London university, Professor James Gow, who had at his disposal a part of the documentation given to him by the Prosecutor's Office and we feel that it is in order and ethical that the witness should base his views on the documents given to him by the party that has called him and it is up to him to choose among those documents those that he considers to be relevant and that is why I object to the proposal made by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have reached a conclusion. You are still making a submission then?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are opposing the application for admitting the documents for the purposes of impeachment, because, as you argued, if I hear you correctly, that the documents themselves are not those which ought to be considered for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have completed my submission. I have nothing more to add. May I go back to my seat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And can we release the witness and thank him for his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was a practice that has been adopted right throughout the Prosecution case, that in cross-examination witnesses were impeached on all range and manner of issues, and at the end of it, there was never any objection raised to the -- well, perhaps I should not say "never", but the documents were put in for that limited purpose and, in my respectful submission, the situation really is no different here -- it is slightly different in the sense of how it may have arisen from case to case, but it does go to that question and I submit, consistent with that approach, they should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will admit it for that limited purpose -- whether the impeachment itself is effective or not is a different matter. If there is sufficient background basis for admitting those documents, I think we will admit it for that purpose. Thank you very much, professor. It has been very pleasant having you and we thank you very much for your time, patience and erudition in explaining many areas which would have ordinarily remained obscure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the next witness now?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before my calling the next witness, I would just like to remind you that this morning I responded to the issue raised by Mr. Niemann regarding the change of the military expert. However, if we had made a mistake for not asking of you specifically the name change, we did notify both the OTP, which had no problems with it, and the Registry and they had no objections. I am now turning to you and asking whether we ought to have asked for a separate permission to call this witness. If we did, our apologies, because we were not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much -- definitely, under the Rules themselves, you should have had leave to do that. I think we will tend to ignore it the purposes for which we are having this hearing. We can accommodate you and you can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I would like now to call the expert witness for the military affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may take your seat. Muhamed VEJZAGIC

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please state your name to the court -- please indicate your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Muhamed Vejzagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vejzagic, before I ask questions to you, with respect to your expert opinions, I would just like to point to a technical matter. In order for the Trial Chamber to be able to follow your testimony, that is my questions and your answers, and in order for all this to be able to be taken down in the transcript, everything that I ask of you and everything that you tell me has to be interpreted. Next to you to the right you will find another headset and you will be able to hear an English interpretation coming through them. When you hear the voice from that headset finishing, that would be the end of the interpretation of my question and then please proceed with the answer. Did you understand me, Mr. Vejzagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vejzagic, can you tell us when you were born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 17 March 1923.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vejzagic, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Livno, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you live currently, Mr. Vejzagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I live in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your professional status currently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a retiree.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, what was your profession during your active years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my active years, I was an officer of the former JNA and then an officer of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- that means that I was a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vejzagic, can you tell me when was it that you first became a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first became a soldier in 1942.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To which army did you belong or to which forces and in which period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1942 I was a member of the Partizan units, which fought the fascism.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did your military career develop after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the wartime, I went to the Soviet Union and attended military schools there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did this training last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It lasted two years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you continue to perform military duties after your training period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I completed training, I continued with my professional service in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this period, did you continue to receive education as an officer of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as a professional soldier, I continued my education. I completed a course for infantry officers which lasted for six months, this was in Sarajevo. I then attended various different courses -- one was for handling the nuclear weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What duties did you perform in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my service in the Yugoslav People's Army, I performed a range of duties starting with the company commander to the detachment commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also engage in teaching during this service period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was also the head of the -- the chief of the school for the infantry officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you also a professor at such a training centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during this period, I also had other duties and I was also a professor in this school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is the highest rank that you acquired in the former Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslav People's Army, I had the rank of a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vejzagic, when did you become a colonel in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I became a colonel in JNA in 1972.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On which duties were you as a colonel in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a colonel of the Yugoslav People's Army, I was transferred to the Territorial Defence, to the republican staff of the Territorial Defence, where I was the chief for programmes for training of officers for Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In which republic of the former SFRY were you assigned to the Territorial Defence department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vejzagic, when did you retire as a colonel of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned at the end of 1980.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vejzagic, did you reactivate yourself at some stage -- some later stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I considered it my duty to become active again, to join the ranks of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which at first was Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vejzagic, what duties did you perform in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina I performed -- I mostly performed the duties in the republican staff in the operations body.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also engage in teaching during this period as you did while you were an active officer of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during my service during the war, there was a need for training the officers' corps for war duties, and there was a need to organise an officers' training centre, a school and that was my duty. I was to organise the operations of the officers' school, to set up the programme and to train the officers who were at the level of company and battalions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where was this school located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This school was located in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vejzagic, since when are you retired again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was retired again in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vejzagic, by performing duties in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you acquire a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during my service in the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I received the rank of Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, during your military career in the former JNA, and later in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you ever receive any military decorations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during my service in the former Yugoslav People's Army, I received 12 decorations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, as a soldier in World War II, did you directly participate in military operations and do you have personal combat experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In World War II, I was a soldier from the start and I do have combat experience -- I did participate in military operations. This kind of experience, a guerrilla type of warfare -- it was within the Partizan units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, after you were reactivated in 1992, during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you directly participate in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During this war of 1992, until the end, I did not directly participate in fighting as an officer -- I was attached to the staff and I was on those staff duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You just said that you were a person who, over a period of 50 years, took part in two wars, so, Brigadier, apart from your military experience and your experience in the war, do you have sufficient experience to be able to form opinions on matters of a military nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can just say that, in both cases, during both wars, these wars were wars against civilians, especially the second one. The first war in which I took part was not as brutal towards civilians as the later one. There were two enemy forces and the fighting went on between the two of them, and so fewer civilians were casualties. However, the development of technology in the intervening period contributed significantly to increasing civilian casualties and we saw this happen in the towns and in protected zones in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, tell me -- a question for you again. When did you retire again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I retired at the end of 1996 -- sorry, not towards the end of 1996 -- in April 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So now we can say that you are a retired brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, even after your retirement, have you actively participated in the matters that relate to the development and strategy of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the general staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina approved an analysis -- a military analysis relating to the experiences of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina between 1992 and 1995. It is a project that involves a large number of contributors. There were prominent experts; four Ph.D.s and three MA candidates are involved in that, a number of generals and high officers are involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did this group cooperate with prominent members of other world armies, that is, experts in this field in preparation of this project?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part we did not cooperate with foreign experts, because we thought that we were doing the analysis for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina based on what happened on the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, I also worked on another project, which was within the "train and equip" programme with gentlemen from the US and I was working on a strategy of defence of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period of 1996 and 1997 and I spent a full year working on this project.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, even though you are a retired Brigadier, you are still active in the research of the military affairs in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am studying the problems that contributed to the dissolution of Yugoslavia and I believe that this is a project that will take a while to finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this long-term research project also involving other aspects besides the military ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This project comprises all areas that relate to the military activities and that is economic aspects and psychological ones in addition to the military ones, the historical ones -- we have 16 parts and there are three chapters of this project. I would not like to elaborate much on this project -- I think it is going to take two or three years to complete it and we would like to gather all relevant notions about the war which we waged for four years, so the military experts would be able to find everything that is relevant about this war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you tell me whether, towards the end of last year, the Defence counsel of Mr. Delalic addressed you with a request to testify in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you immediately accept the Defence's request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was unable to accept immediately, before thinking over my role, and before reviewing the area which was to become the question of my testimony and then I had to study also my possibilities, whether I would be up to such a task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Brigadier, that, at the end of January, or rather the beginning of February, you finally accepted to be an expert witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, will you please tell us what did you rely upon in preparing your expert report, or, rather, what will you rely upon for your testimony in this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My expert opinion is mainly based on my familiarity with the facts as a professional officer, that is, my expertise, my long-standing career in the former army, and the experiences I gained in this war. Secondly, I relied on materials, publications, that I gained access to in the course of my research in preparation for this expert testimony relating to this last war. Thirdly, I relied on documents that I was able to gain possession of while working on this task, that is, the documents from the former Yugoslavia -- that is part of the documents -- and then also documents that were compiled -- rather, the normative acts of the former Yugoslavia, those relating to Defence drafted by the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then, also, all other materials that I had access to from various symposiums, publications that also dealt with this war and this time period from 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
