utterances.text: Brigadier, could you please tell me who was it that made it possible for you to gain access to the documents that you have just mentioned, and which you reviewed before compiling your expert report, that is, what are the sources from which you obtained those documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me say first that it is partly the archives of the general staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then the archives of the Institute for the Investigation of War Crimes, then also all other materials that I was able to collect in the municipal staff in Konjic, documents that I obtained from the court in Mostar. That is more or less the sources from which I drew data for the preparation of my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, is it true that the office of the Defence also placed at your disposal a certain number of documents that you may have used or not, but you gained insight into them when compiling your expert opinion and report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I omitted to mention that -- that is true, I also used those materials.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, did you, too, engage in certain research in the territory of Konjic, or in the institutions that exist today in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I studied in all the institutions that exist in Konjic today any materials relevant to this case and, also, any information I could obtain from other witnesses, but I do apologise, I am not a general, please -- let me correct you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Brigadiers do like to be called generals -- brigadier-general.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that could be a rank, because this is a new rank in our army which we did not have before, and, in view of all that you have said about your knowledge and experience, maybe that title would suit you better, but I will call you correctly and I apologise for my mistake. So, Brigadier, will you tell us, when compiling your expert opinion, did you review any videotapes in the possession of TV stations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I reviewed videotapes, especially those relating to Konjic, from which one could see quite well the situation in Konjic, especially the shelling of the town, the casualties among the population. I also saw the suffering of the prisoners in prison. I saw inhabitants waiting in line to receive humanitarian aid. I saw an empty supermarket with nothing on the stalls, et cetera, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, after all that you have told us as being the basis of your research and studies, could you tell this Trial Chamber that you did collect sufficient reliable information and documents for you to be able to give a complete and impartial opinion and testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could say that one can never have enough research, but I do think that I collected sufficient evidence to be able to be impartial and testify about what I have included in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We should now, Brigadier, go to discussing the issues dealt with in your expert report and to tackle directly the problem of greatest interest to this Trial Chamber, that is, the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Konjic in 1992. With a view brief questions, let us refer to the short period that preceded that time for a better understanding of your report. Could you, Brigadier, please, explain to us, in concise form, the organisation and structure of the armed forces in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The armed forces of the former Yugoslavia consisted of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence. These were two components. The Yugoslav People's Army, as the armed force, in the doctrine of use, was intended to be used at the beginning of an aggression to prevent incursions. It was technically well equipped with state of the art equipment and its task was to take upon itself the first blow and thereby to ensure the mobilisation of the reserve force of the army and the Territorial Defence. According to the concept of the defence of the country, a new structure was set in place as of 1962, that is, after the events in Czechoslovakia and a Territorial Defence was formed. Conceptually it was designed as being on the ground and in collaboration with the armed forces of the army, to participate in the country's defence. Thank you. The substance of its very existence was that we had envisaged that we would not be able to resist a technically superior power of modern armies, so the possibility was envisaged for the Yugoslav People's Army to abandon territory up to a certain point and the Territorial Defence remains in the rear and its task was to engage in struggle behind the enemy lines, to prevent communication, to prevent supplies, to inflict losses on the enemy, and in any event such a conception of the country's defence was such that regardless of the fact that the operational army abandoned territory, that territory would not remain empty -- where the army had left a part of the forces would remain and those were the Territorial Defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With this question, you have conveyed the initial statements contained in your report. May I ask you now, Brigadier, after this research, did you compile a written report and send a copy to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May the witness now be shown his report? Before that, is your report accompanied by documents that have been put into three volumes of this kind (indicating)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would first like to ask these volumes to be marked for identification. This is folder 1 -- there are sufficient copies for the witness and the court and then, together with the witness, we can identify this material of his so that we can all follow his testimony (Handed). This is volume 1, could it be the first to be marked for identification and given to the witness and the Trial Chamber. Could a copy of number 1 be given to the judges -- the Prosecutor has already been served with a copy, and could I have the number that the exhibit has been marked with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You mean the report itself is in three volumes, is it, or are they annexes to the report?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, your Honours. The first volume in the front is the report itself and this is followed by annexes, and there are nine of them, so the expert witness will first examine his report and identify it and then the annexes contained in these folders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose that is my own conjecture, too, that she should have his report and then followed by the annexes -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is why I asked this first volume to be given to you, because at the beginning of that volume is the expert report, which we will have identified first, and it is followed by annexes starting from number 1 onwards. That is why I am not distributing the second volume until the expert witness identifies his expert report.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This has been marked exhibit D143/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, can you please open this binder? Will you tell me, please, whether, at the beginning of this folder, you find the expert report compiled by you after completing the research you have told us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell me whether you have in your copy a Bosnian version of the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To facilitate the task of the witness, because we have given copies to the court in English, may I ask you, your Honours, to be permitted to give the witness a part of the same report in the Bosnian language, because of course he could not bring his own copy into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you have the leave of the Trial Chamber to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. (Handed). Is that the expert report that you compiled, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to your expert report, are there annexes 1 to 9 consisting of the documentation that you used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say, Brigadier, that you used, in preparing this report, a part of the documents of Dr. Calic, who was an expert witness before this Trial Chamber, and that, accompanying your report, you indicated which of those documents you had used and included among your own documents from Dr. Calic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the witness has recognised his report, and as it will serve as the basis for his testimony, I should like to tender it into evidence immediately, and I assume that you will make your ruling after the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not expect -- my application is that it be moved into evidence at the end of cross-examination, because of the difficulties that we have explained earlier. Certainly, there is no problem with it being used and referred to throughout the course of the testimony of this witness. I do not envisage any difficulties, but I do see it as being more efficient if we are given the time to fully study it and then come back to the Chamber and then possibly reduce any objections to an absolute minimum. I think it would be a far more efficient process. That may be what Madam Residovic has just said -- I am not sure that she is actually moving its admission now, just making that observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the witness can continue to refer to his document as we go along. It will not affect it being used for the purpose of his evidence. He can use it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It has not been formally tendered, but it does not mean he cannot refer to it. He is allowed to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, is it true that this first volume entitled "one" and has now been marked by the court contains, in addition to your own finding, annexes with documents marked as annex 1, 2 and 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask that the other annexes be also marked for identification, so that they may be used during the testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This has been marked volume 2, D144/1, and volume 3, D145/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Brigadier, that this second folder of documents that you relied upon when compiling your opinion contains annex 4, annex 5A and annex 5B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It contains annex 4, 5 and 5B.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Brigadier, that the third volume contains documents marked as 5B -- 5D, annex 6, 7, 8 and 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it contains all these annexes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since your expert opinion has been marked together with the supporting material, we can now move to the questions contained in your expert analysis. Since you told us what the organisation and the structure of the military in the former Yugoslavia was, can you please tell us how the JNA was organised as relative to the federal constitutional arrangements in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Parallel with the State structure, the army was organised into armies, which were based in the republics. Each republic had its own headquarters of the army in its capital.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did a change occur at some point in time in the army organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the organisation of the army was changed towards the end of 1988.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened then, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The armies were abolished then and army areas were introduced.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there general agreement for such a reorganisation of the army into army districts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, instead of the armies, four military districts were formed -- Zagreb, Belgrade, Split and Skopje. With the abolition of the armies, Slovenia and its State leadership opposed this, believing that, by moving the headquarters of an army from Ljubljana was not a good idea, and that is why they intervened with the general staff and with the political structures and the central authorities in Belgrade, but they were unable to change anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to the events that we will be discussing, were there any military reasons for such a reorganisation of the army, or were political plans behind it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For such a reorganisation of the armed forces, there certainly were no military reasons, because no danger threatened Yugoslavia and no particular improvement in defence was achieved by this reorganisation, but there were political gains behind it all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did such an organisation of the army strengthen the military and political influence of some of the centres in the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the army reorganisation, the real motive was for the army leadership, that is, the army commands, to escape -- to be drawn outside the influence of republican leaderships, so that, should the need arise, the republican leaderships could have no influence over the command of the army and its possible use.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in view of your duties in the army and in the Territorial Defence, could you tell me whether the Territorial Defence was a significant force within the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence as a component of the armed forces was, in those days, when it reached a peak somewhere in 1985, it was a highly developed armed force. For example, in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was almost three times as numerous as the Sarajevo army. It numbered about 320,000 men, mostly under arms. However, in its structure, the equipment was not so developed as it was in the operative army. The army had three branches -- the ground forces, the air force and the navy. Within the framework of the ground forces, in addition to the infantry, there were the armoured mechanised units, the artillery; in other words, all the latest forms of equipment were represented. The Territorial Defence was something else -- it had a predominantly infantry composition, with some logistic support, that is light artillery, mostly mortars, recoiler guns, because, by the nature of its use behind the enemy lines it could not use heavy artillery -- it did not have any armoured units or vehicles, its manoeuvring was carried out mostly on foot, and on horseback, so that the aim of this component of the armed forces was never intended to have heavy artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would now move on, but perhaps this is a good time to adjourn for today, so that we can resume work tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, we can adjourn now and resume at 10 a.m. tomorrow. The Trial Chamber will now rise. 7 8 9 11 12 13 14 15

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: at 5.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of April 1998, at 10 a.m.
